Press Release:


Epilepsy
Radical medical advancements in the treatment of epilepsy are giving sufferers a chance at a seizure-free life. Carte Blanche investigates procedures like White Matter Tractography which allows neurosurgeons to navigate a road map of a patient’s brain like never before. And, Neurobionic Prediction Implants that alert a sufferer to imminent seizures.
Producer: ABC, Australia


Script:


Thursday, 4 September 2014
Epilepsy
Mark Horstman reveals the advancements in epilepsy treatment that are giving epilepsy sufferers new hope.
NARRATION
Epilepsy is a brain disorder where abnormal electrical activity causes persistent seizures, affecting 1 in 100 people worldwide. Epilepsy is the second most common neurological disease after stroke. In the past, treatment options were limited, but now two important advances in both detecting epileptic seizures and their surgical treatment offer sufferers new hope. Oliver and Joey are identical twins. They share the same DNA, but there's one key difference - Oliver has chronic epilepsy.

Kimberly Terrell
We were a little bit worried about Ollie when he was born, but it was only when he was five hours old that we realised he was in trouble. He'd had a stroke around about the time that he was born, and we were told that he would have cerebral palsy affecting his right-hand side, and that he was at a higher risk of developing epilepsy.

NARRATION
And that's what happened when Oliver was just three years old. The stroke that hit Oliver at birth caused a cavity to form in the left hemisphere of his brain. The scar tissue surrounding this cavity caused his nerve cells to fire electrical signals erratically, generating a lightning storm inside his brain.

Mark Terrell
I think most people think of epilepsy as the grand mal seizures, where people sort of fall on the floor and twitching. It's not like... It hasn't been like that.

Kimberly Terrell
Hey, Ollie. Are you gonna bang the table?

Kimberly Terrell
Before epilepsy started, he was an amazing concentrater for his age, and he basically started rolling all over the ground, slamming into the furniture on purpose. So, we really struggled with the fact that our kid, who was on the most fantastic trajectory, suddenly wasn't socially appropriate, wasn't concentrating, wasn't learning.

NARRATION
Without treatment, Oliver's epilepsy will get worse. At the age of five, he already wears a helmet to protect him from seizures that cause him to lose consciousness and fall to the ground. But even worse than that are the learning problems he will face.

Kimberly Terrell
We've been told that he'll probably end up at a special school, unable to learn, because the epilepsy has such a disorganising impact on his brain, and this is a bright little boy.

Mark Horstman
At the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, there's a new method for studying the brains of children, and it gives epilepsy sufferers like Oliver a much better chance at a life free of seizures.

Dr Wirginia Maixner
Oliver's stroke caused significant scarring in the brain, and that then is generating seizures in Oliver's brain. It has really severe implications for his brain for two reasons. One is that, with the seizures that he's having, it means that he has abnormal firing in the brain, but similarly, just the medications alone that we need to give Oliver to try and control the seizures, in fact have a negative effect on his development.

NARRATION
Oliver's story is a common one. Around one third of all epilepsy sufferers gain little or no relief from modern medications, many of which have serious side effects.

Mark Horstman
So, what's the long-term solution for him?

Dr Wirginia Maixner
The long-term solution is surgery. Somebody like Oliver, in the past, we would do what we call a hemispherectomy, which is where you either remove or disconnect the whole of his left side of his brain.

NARRATION
While this technique does stop epileptic seizures, it also destroys a lot of brain function.

Dr Wirginia Maixner
So, where technology has changed in the last five years or so has been the development of what we call tractography.

Dr Marc Seal
White matter tractography is like a road map to the brain. We look at the highways, we look at the narrow streets. We get a sense of how the brain parts are connected to each other, and how they're changing with time.

NARRATION
These highways and narrow streets are commonly known as the brain's white matter tracts - tightly packed bundles of nerve fibres that connect and communicate between parts of the brain. With a standard MRI scan, they're impossible to see, but there is a way.

Dr Marc Seal
What we measure is we measure the flow of water through the brain.

NARRATION
Water molecules are constantly moving in the brain. They never stop - it's called diffusion. In most parts of the brain, including the grey matter, the movement of the water is random, but inside the white matter tracts the water moves directionally. Using an MRI scan, the direction of the water flow can be calculated, and the brain's true complexity revealed. Dr Joseph Yang was the lead researcher in developing the tractography techniques used here, and also personally responsible for plotting the tractography for Oliver's brain.

Mark Horstman
So, what's this a picture of?

Dr Joseph Yang
So, Mark, this is a picture of Oliver's brain. We're looking from feet up. That's the left side of his brain, this is the right side. And to show that these are actually the areas we're going to target for surgery tomorrow.

Mark Horstman
That's what you have to remove?

Dr Joseph Yang
Exactly.

Mark Horstman
OK, but how do you know if they're getting too close to the white matter, the white tracts of the brain?

Dr Joseph Yang
Before we are able to do tractography, there is absolutely no way you can tell exactly where the nerve fibre tracts are.

Mark Horstman
Until now.

Dr Joseph Yang
Until now.

Dr Joseph Yang
So, with the click of a button...

Mark Horstman
That's a whole new level of detail now.

Dr Joseph Yang
Exactly. We can change the angle a bit. Now we're looking...

NARRATION
In Oliver's case, the sensitive nerve tracts that control both the movement of the right side of his body and his vision run right through the area of brain tissue that needs to be removed. Before tractography, this kind of surgery would have been extremely risky.

NARRATION
It's the day of the surgery, and Oliver and his family are making their way to the operating theatre. It's going to be a long day. Surgery like this can take anywhere from 4 to 14 hours.

Dr Wirginia Maixner
Before we even go into the operating theatre, I already study on the tractography that Joseph, our PhD research person, has done, and I already have a mental image in my mind where those tracts are lying. What we then do is we take that information and we marry it up to an MRI scan that we do during the surgery.

Mark Horstman
This is the only paediatric hospital in Australia, and one of the few in the world, where they can do MRI scans in the operating theatre. That means that the neurosurgeons can see changes in the brain straightaway.

Dr Wirginia Maixner
What it gives me, as the surgeon, is I can be very, very precise in where I am and where I need to be, and I can then operate and know exactly where the pathways are around that, and it means I can preserve function, and that's the huge difference.

NARRATION
Right now, Wirginia is preparing to carefully open the left side of Oliver's brain.

Mark Horstman
Just like dodgy wiring with bad insulation that causes short circuits, that scar tissue is the focus of his epileptic seizures. The challenge here today is to remove that scar tissue without damaging the nerve tracts that run right alongside it.

NARRATION
Oliver's surgery has every promise of success, and we'll be back to visit him in the next few months to see how he's getting on. For many epilepsy sufferers, though, even the most revolutionary brain surgery is not an option. For those patients for whom surgery is not appropriate, a more experimental treatment called neurobionics is taking shape at St Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne.

Professor Mark Cook
Surgery's suitable for some people, but nowhere near as many as we thought, either because the abnormalities that are causing the seizures are too big or in areas that are too hard for us to get to safely. So, that's been a big problem. So, neurobionics is linking brains and nerves to machines, essentially.

NARRATION
One person who received a neurobionic implant was Hannah Galvin.

Hannah Galvin
It started off when I was 16. I'd had a big day at dancing, and I ended up on the ground. And then I woke up in hospital, and asked my dad what epilepsy was.

Professor Mark Cook
And we wondered whether we could treat Hannah better with medications, and we tried a lot of other medications, and unfortunately we didn't make much progress, because she had terrible side effects from the tablets, I'd have to say, and so she seemed a really good candidate for the seizure prediction system.

NARRATION
Developed by Mark Cook and his team, the seizure prediction system consists of an implant under the skin that actually tracks and alerts the user when they're about to have an epileptic seizure.

Professor Mark Cook
So, these are the electrodes that we put inside the brain. And these were inserted directly over the surface of the brain, recording the seizure activity, and this long wire is tunnelled down under the skin just below the collarbone, and then the actual device, which records and transmits the information, is implanted under the skin here too, much like a heart pacemaker.

NARRATION
Placed within the brain, the electrode picks up electrical activity and sends it to the implant, which, in turn, sends it wirelessly to a receiver that lets the user know that a seizure is imminent.

Professor Mark Cook
A series of lights across the top tells the patient there's either high or moderate or very low risk of seizures.

NARRATION
In most patients, the seizure prediction system was a complete success, but not for Hannah.

Hannah Galvin
The surprise in the red light was, 'Wow, I seizure quite a bit.' I wasn't aware of the amount of seizures I had. I thought that it just wasn't working properly.

NARRATION
While Hannah's implant never stopped predicting seizures, she was simply having too many for the device to be effective.

Mark Horstman
What if an implant could trigger a device to release drugs directly to where you need that medication?

Hannah Galvin
Well, that would be perfect. It's just not available yet.

NARRATION
Not quite yet, but Mark Cook and his team are already moving to the next phase of their neurobionic research.

Mark Horstman
Mark, how similar is epilepsy in rats to epilepsy in humans?

Professor Mark Cook
Different types of epilepsy in rats, but some rats have epilepsy which is identical to that in humans, and these particular rats, they have seizures which are just like human seizures, and during that time, we can test our new treatments on them.

NARRATION
The treatment being tested here is the targeted delivery of anti-convulsant medication directly into the rats' brains via tiny pieces of drug-infused polymer.

Professor Mark Cook
They're very small particles. So, this is some of the polymer at the bottom of this tube here. So, they're just like dust, or very small plastic sheets, that contain the drug at the moment. Because we know exactly where these seizures are from, we can put a little deposit of a polymer that slowly releases an anti-convulsant drug in there, and recently we've demonstrated that we can use this to stop their seizures, so this is really exciting.

NARRATION
Because the application is so targeted, it promises to increase the effectiveness and reduce the side effects of taking epilepsy medications.

Professor Mark Cook
So, what we are hoping to do, ultimately, is connect these sorts of bionic systems so that the device, which is detecting, or even predicting events, is connected to a polymer like this, releasing very small amounts of drug directly to the brain only when it's needed.

Mark Horstman
It's nearly two months since the operation, and Oliver's back at home with his family. The combination of the surgery, guided by the tractography, has meant a dramatic transformation in his life. But watch where you're going.

Kimberly Terrell
It's been about seven weeks since Ollie's surgery. The night of the surgery, Ollie gave us kisses and said single words to us - he was still very groggy - and by about two days after the surgery, he was just bright and sparky. There's been a big physical recovery, but it's been pretty obvious to us that there's no seizure activity and that the concentration and the clarity that we did the surgery for, that it's here already.

Mark Terrell
It'll be two years from the surgery before we can be sure whether he's completely cured, but so far, so good, and we're really, really happy with how he's going so far.

Mark Horstman
And what did Dr Wirginia do?

Oliver Terrell
Put my seizures in the bin.

Mark Horstman
They put your seizures where?

Oliver Terrell
In the bin!

NARRATION
Inside Oliver's brain, and the brains of hundreds of other recipients of tractography-guided surgery, the storm has quietened. This young boy's future, just like the future of epilepsy treatment, is looking promising indeed.
